title: You didn’t stumble into Ezekiel’s visions by accident.
paragraphs: You didn’t stumble into Ezekiel’s visions by accident.
Something in you recognizes the weight of them—the strangeness, the fire, the wheels, the creatures—and part of you wonders if it’s too much to understand… or too dangerous to ignore.
Because it is.
Ezekiel doesn’t read like a calm devotional. It feels like interruption. Like heaven breaking into a world that thought it was fine.
And that’s exactly what it is.

Ezekiel was standing among exiles—people who thought they still belonged to God while living like He didn’t matter. Jerusalem was collapsing, but they kept believing everything would be okay. Religion was still there. Ritual was still there.
But God was not impressed.
Then the sky opened.
“I looked, and behold, a stormy wind came out of the north, and a great cloud, with brightness around it, and fire flashing continually…” (Ezekiel 1:4)
This wasn’t poetry for entertainment. This was confrontation.
The first vision—the living creatures, the wheels within wheels, eyes everywhere—was not meant to be decoded like a puzzle. It was meant to destroy Ezekiel’s illusion of control.
God was showing him something terrifyingly simple:
He is not limited.

Not by geography.
Not by temple walls.
Not by human expectations.
Israel thought God belonged in Jerusalem. But here He was, revealing His glory in Babylon—among exiles, among judgment, among people who had already crossed lines they couldn’t undo.
The wheels weren’t random.
They moved in every direction without turning.
Meaning God doesn’t need to adjust Himself to your situation.
He already sees every direction at once.
The eyes covering the wheels?
Nothing escapes Him.

Not the public version of you.
Not the private version.
Not the thoughts you rehearsed but never said.

God saw it.
You knew.
And that’s where the discomfort starts.
Because Ezekiel’s visions don’t just describe God’s power—they expose human rebellion.
“Son of man, I send you to the people of Israel, to nations of rebels, who have rebelled against me…” (Ezekiel 2:3)
Not confused. Not misinformed.
Rebellious.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
The terrifying visions aren’t the final message.
They are the setup.
Because once God shatters your illusion of control, once He exposes your sin clearly enough that you can’t excuse it anymore, He does something unexpected.
He speaks hope into what should have been a closed case.
You see it in the valley.
Dry bones.
Not weak bones. Not injured bones.
Dead.
“The hand of the Lord was upon me… and set me down in the middle of the valley; it was full of bones… and behold, they were very dry.” (Ezekiel 37:1–2)
This is not recovery.
This is impossibility.
And God asks a question that cuts deeper than logic:
“Son of man, can these bones live?” (Ezekiel 37:3)
That question isn’t just for Ezekiel.
It’s for you.
Because you’ve seen parts of your life that feel just like that valley.

Habits you can’t break.
Sin you keep returning to.
A heart that feels harder than it used to be.
Externally functioning. Internally dry.
Then God does what no system, no self-help, no religion can do.
He speaks.
“Behold, I will cause breath to enter you, and you shall live.” (Ezekiel 37:5)
Breath.
The same breath from the beginning.
The same breath humanity lost in its rebellion.
The same breath that only God can give back.
And suddenly, the bones come together. Flesh forms. Life returns.
But don’t miss it—
They didn’t revive themselves.
They didn’t collaborate with God.
They responded to His Word.
This is where the Gospel has been hiding in plain sight the entire time.
Because Ezekiel’s visions are not just about judgment…
They are about resurrection.
“I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you… And I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh.” (Ezekiel 36:26)
You don’t fix your heart.
God replaces it.
And He didn’t do that through effort.
He did it through Jesus Christ.
Because the same God Ezekiel saw in terrifying glory stepped into flesh, walked among sinners, and took judgment upon Himself.
“But he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities…” (Isaiah 53:5)
The fire Ezekiel saw?
Jesus stepped into it.
The judgment Israel deserved?
Jesus absorbed it.
The separation your sin created?
Jesus closed it with His blood.
So now the question isn’t whether God is powerful enough.
Ezekiel already answered that.
The question is whether you will keep pretending you’re alive when you know something in you is still dry.
You’ve heard truth before.
You’ve felt conviction before.
You’ve said “one day” before.
But the valley doesn’t fix itself with time.
Only God’s voice brings life.
And He’s still speaking.
If something in you is stirring right now, that’s not random. That’s not emotion.
That’s confrontation mixed with mercy.
You don’t need more information.
You need resurrection.
Turn.
Not gradually. Not later.
Now.
Call sin what it is. Lay it down. Stop negotiating with it.
Trust in Jesus Christ—not as an idea, not as a backup plan—but as your only hope.
Because there are only two directions from here:

Stay in the valley and get used to being dry…
Or respond to His voice and live.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior
Stay with it.
